pronunciation.approximation: Say "radagast" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Radagast".

kin.label: Old Slavic
kin.form: Radogostъ, the form behind Thietmar of Merseburg's Latin 'Radigost' — attested only in medieval Latin chronicles, never in a Slavic source

kin.label: Proto-Slavic
kin.form: *radъ 'glad, willing' + *gostь 'guest' — the traditional analysis, 'he who gladly receives guests', matching the hospitality domain (Trubachev; Máchal)

kin.label: Modern literary
kin.form: Radagast, the anglicized spelling naturalized into English by Tolkien's wizard in The Hobbit (1937)

pronunciation.note: Radagast is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized name is pure ASCII — no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. The doubled-a spelling is a scholarly convention descending from Thietmar's 'Radigost'; only the capital distinguishes temple from plain text.

domains.title: Radagast
domains.subtitle: Hospitality
domains.lead: Radagast — medieval Radigost — was the chief god of the Redarii, a Slavic people between the Elbe and the Oder, worshipped in a great wooden temple-city called Radgosc. His name ties him to the guest and the glad welcome: he is the god of hospitality, of the open door, of beasts, and of the trust between strangers.

cards.name: The Temple of Radgosc
cards.desc: Thietmar of Merseburg describes the god's vast wooden temple-city, the religious capital of the Elbe Slavs (Chronicon VI.23–25).

cards.name: The God of Guests
cards.desc: His name — Proto-Slavic *radъ-gostь, 'glad guest' or 'he who gladly receives' — makes hospitality itself a divine office.

cards.name: The Oracle
cards.desc: Adam of Bremen reports that Radgosc gave answers to all the Slavic peoples — and even to Christian Saxons.

cards.name: A Fragile Monument
cards.desc: The temple burned around 1068; what survives of Radagast is the witness of three chroniclers and a borrowed wizard.

symbols.name: The bronze doors
symbols.meaning: Adam of Bremen reports the Radgosc temple's bronze doors — the threshold between the god's house and the world.

symbols.name: The hung weapons
symbols.meaning: Shields and spears of the Redarii dedicated on the temple walls, a West Slavic arsenal of vows.

symbols.name: The carved oracle
symbols.meaning: The god's answers cut into wood and carried home by those who consulted him across the north.

symbols.name: The helmeted image
symbols.meaning: The cult statue of Radigost that stood foremost among the temple's many images, in armor befitting a god of the assembly.

symbols.name: The tribal standard
symbols.meaning: The banner kept in the god's house, carried to war only after the oracle had been consulted.

mythology.lead: Radagast is known almost entirely from three medieval chroniclers — Thietmar of Merseburg, Adam of Bremen, and Helmold of Bosau — writing two to four centuries after the god's heyday. No Slavic myth of him survives in his own language; what follows are the historical episodes that medieval writers themselves treated as his legend.

myths.title: Radgosc, the God Among the Lakes
myths.text: Our earliest witness is an enemy. Thietmar of Merseburg, bishop and chronicler, wrote in book VI of his Chronicon (c. 1012–1018) about Riedegost — the Germans called it Radgosc — the chief seat of the Redarii, a Slavic people between the Elbe and the Oder. There stood a vast wooden temple, heaped with the offerings of many tribes, and in it the image of the god who gave the city his name: Radigost. Thietmar wrote with open contempt — he was a soldier of the Church that wanted this cult destroyed — which is precisely why his testimony matters: a propagandist does not invent the power of what he attacks. Radgosc was not a village shrine but a confederate sanctuary, the religious capital of the Elbe Slavs, where tribes that quarreled in peacetime met in the god's shadow. The myth Radagast never got to tell survives as architecture: a god whose legend is a great wooden hall, and whose worship was the politics of a people.

myths.title: Answers Carved in Wood
myths.text: Adam of Bremen, writing his history of the Hamburg church some sixty years later (Gesta Hammaburgensis II.18, c. 1075), adds what Thietmar omits: the oracle. Radgosc, Adam says, was consulted by all the Slavic peoples; the god answered, and the answers were carved and carried home to govern war and settlement alike. His temple had bronze doors and walls hung with weapons — an arsenal of vows. Helmold of Bosau (Chronica Slavorum I.2, c. 1170) supplies the scandalous coda: even Christian Saxons consulted the oracle, crossing the religious frontier the Church was drawing. An oracle crosses borders because necessity does — the god of a single tribe can be refused, but a god who answers the questions everyone must ask cannot. Radagast's carved judgments made him the judge of peoples who shared no language but his: in the eleventh-century north, a Slavic god sat for a while on the throne of uncertainty where every nation seeks counsel.

myths.title: The Temple Falls
myths.text: The chronicle of the god's end is brief. Adam of Bremen records that the temple of Radgosc burned — around 1068, in the Saxon margraves' wars against the Elbe Slavs, as the empire pushed its frontier eastward with sword and baptism. With the hall went the oracle, the standard, and whatever priesthood kept the god's house. No Slavic lament for Radagast survives — no Slavic chronicle survives at all — so the burning is known only from the winning side, in the flat tone with which victors note a difficulty removed. Yet the destruction was the making of the god's legend: a cult that had concentrated the wealth and allegiance of a confederation went up in a single campaign, and what could not be burned was the name. Read backwards through the smoke, the fire is Radagast's passion — the moment when hospitality's door was nailed shut, and the god became a guest in other people's stories.

myths.title: Tolkien's Wizard
myths.text: The god's second life began in a library. Jacob Grimm carried the name Radagost into European scholarship in his Teutonic Mythology (1835), and J. R. R. Tolkien — who knew his Grimm — borrowed it for a wizard. In The Hobbit (1937) Radagast the Brown is the master of shapes and changes of hue, the friend of beasts and birds, the lover of herbs; and Tolkien later observed that he had taken the name from an old Slavic deity, liking its legendary sound. The borrowing was truer than invention could have been: Tolkien's hermit of the wild, who forgets councils of war to tend wounded animals, is a portrait of the god the etymologists reconstruct — radъ, glad; gostь, guest — the one who gladly receives. More people today know Radagast as a wizard than ever knew him as a god; the burned temple survives, improbably, as a footnote in a children's tale, and the god of hospitality lives on as the friendliest face in Middle-earth.

lore.syncretism: Medieval writers and modern scholars alike have tried to fold Radagast into wider patterns. Later philology asked whether Radigost was a name or a title, and whether the god of Radgosc was the West Slavic counterpart of Svantevit, the great armed oracle-god of Rügen described by Saxo Grammaticus — the identification is speculation resting mostly on the shared profile of a tribal war-oracle. The chroniclers performed a syncretism in reverse, reading the wooden temple as a demonic parody of the Church's own shrines. In the nineteenth century Grimm's Teutonic Mythology rescued the name for comparative philology; in the twentieth Tolkien naturalized it into English fantasy; and modern Slavic neopaganism now restores Radogost to worship, usually as a god of hospitality, animals, and the road — a reconstruction built, honestly enough, on three hostile chronicles and a borrowed wizard.
lore.culturalLegacy: For scholarship, Radagast is the best-attested god of the Polabian Slavs — a whole people's religion compressed into three Latin chronicles. His name keeps surfacing wherever Slavic studies meet popular culture: in Tolkien's wizard, in neopagan rites, in the reconstructed temple at Groß Raden that thousands visit each year. The hospitality he was named for survives in the living Slavic word for guest — gost — and in its cousins across Europe, host and guest, all from the same Indo-European root. Restoring Radagast to Unicode restores a name the Church tried to burn out of memory, and that a philologist's imagination carried to the ends of Middle-earth.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Radagast is the patron of everything we almost lost. His entire dossier comes from men who wanted him gone — a bishop, two monks, writing the god into extinction — and yet the name refused to die, surfacing three centuries later on the lips of a fantasy writer who liked its sound. There is a lesson in that: worship is louder than witnesses, and a god of hospitality is especially hard to kill, because hospitality is the one divine office every culture keeps open.

He also asks an uncomfortable question of the scholarly record. When a people's own voices are silenced, what remains is the enemies' paperwork — and we build temples of the imagination on it anyway. Radagast's temple is real now precisely because it is contested: nobody's property, everybody's guest. That, in the end, is the meaning of his name. The god who gladly receives survives by being received — by chroniclers, by philologists, by children who never heard of the Redarii and love the wizard anyway.

lore.archaeology: No certain site of Radgosc has been identified, and the candidates lie in the lakeland between the Elbe and the Oder — the region of Neubrandenburg in Mecklenburg has been proposed. The open-air museum at Groß Raden (Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) reconstructs a fortified Slavic temple of exactly the type the chroniclers describe, though its identification with Rethra is traditional rather than proven. Excavations at other West Slavic cult centers — Starigard/Oldenburg in Wagria, Brandenburg an der Havel, and the Arkona headland on Rügen — have yielded wooden idols, temple rings, cult standards, and post-built hall sanctuaries of the tenth to twelfth centuries that match the chronicles' picture of a wealthy, wood-built religion. The material record and the written one agree on the essentials: a god housed in a great timber hall, attended by weapons, standards, and an oracle.
